name: HMB
lead: HMB (beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate) is a metabolite of the essential amino acid leucine that the body produces naturally; roughly 5 percent of dietary leucine is converted to it [4]. Two supplement forms have been studied, a calcium salt (HMB-Ca) and a free acid (HMB-FA) [1].

It is marketed to lifters and athletes for reducing muscle damage and muscle protein breakdown and for supporting recovery, and it is also used in clinical oral nutritional supplements for older and ill patients [1][5][6].

The research picture differs by population. The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) position stand states that HMB's proposed mode of action is a dual effect, enhancing muscle protein synthesis and suppressing breakdown, and that chronic intake appears safe for up to at least a year [1]. Meta-analyses in trained athletes report small effects, while results in older adults and in clinical conditions are more often positive but vary by study [2][7].
infobox: Dietary supplement; also used in medical nutrition products

paras: HMB is taken by resistance trainers and endurance athletes, especially during periods of heavy training volume, to try to limit muscle damage. T Nation members describe adding HMB to stacks to cope with training volume or recover faster [12][13][14]. It also appears in stacks of users who combine it with other supplements and, in some posts, with prescribed hormonal therapies [15].
HMB is an ingredient in specialized oral nutritional supplements studied in malnourished older adults, sarcopenia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cancer and bed rest [5][6][8][9][10][11].

A 2018 meta-analysis of randomised trials in trained and competitive athletes examined strength and body composition outcomes [2]. A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis assessed muscle loss in older adults [7]. The ISSN 2025 position stand summarised the field and concluded among other points that HMB may help reduce muscle damage and promote recovery [1].
A review of HMB in healthy and muscle-wasting conditions in 2017 discussed results across populations [16]. A 2022 systematic review examined HMB in patients with cancer [17].

Trials that combined HMB with other nutrients include a trial of a specialized oral nutritional supplement with dietary counselling in community-dwelling older adults at risk of malnutrition [5] and a multicentre trial of a high-protein HMB supplement on readmission and mortality in hospitalised malnourished older adults [6]. Because these are multi-ingredient products, the contribution of HMB cannot be separated.

The ISSN position stand states that available safety and toxicity data suggest chronic HMB-Ca and HMB-FA use is safe for up to at least one year and that HMB does not negatively affect glucose tolerance or insulin sensitivity [1].

HMB is produced when leucine is converted to alpha-ketoisocaproate and then partly to HMB; most dietary leucine follows other metabolic routes [4]. The ISSN statement reports that HMB-FA appears to raise blood HMB more than HMB-Ca, though recent results are mixed [1].

The primary mechanism proposed is a combined stimulation of muscle protein synthesis and suppression of protein breakdown, and the ISSN notes that HMB activates mTORC1 independently of the leucine-sensing Sestrin2-GATOR2 pathway [1]. A 2013 study compared the effects of leucine and HMB on human skeletal muscle protein metabolism [18].

HMB was marketed in the late 1990s and early 2000s in bodybuilding magazines and by supplement companies. T Nation threads from that period include members asking whether HMB was 'as good as Deca' and recalling saving money to buy 'super-advanced' HMB products alongside brands such as Myoplex, and one member described it as the start of a downfall for a prominent supplement figure, in the poster's view [19][20][21]. A later poster recalled an HMB study in which subjects were said to gain more than from steroids [22]. Forum members' present-day views range from adding HMB to regimens to saying most supplements add little beyond training, sleep and nutrition [23][12].
Meta-analyses: trained athletes (2018) [2], older adults muscle loss (2015) [7]. Position stand: ISSN (2025) [1].

Randomised trials include a sarcopenia trial of HMB supplementation in older adults [9], a crossover trial of creatine plus HMB on functional strength independent of muscle mass in physically active older adults [10], a trial of omega-3 with and without HMB in COPD [11], and a 10-day bed rest study of HMB and lean body mass in older adults [8]. A 2022 systematic review considered cancer patients [17].

Registered trials include HMB in resistance-trained men (NCT01508338), in older women (NCT02118181), lung transplant candidates in rehabilitation (NCT07660991), hemodialysis patients (NCT01837238), ACL surgery recovery (NCT02602561), Crohn's disease with sarcopenia (NCT07171593), and cerebral palsy (NCT05384951) [25][26][27][28][29][30][31].

lore.intro: HMB has been discussed on T Nation since the early 2000s, first as a heavily marketed muscle supplement and later as a minor add-on to training stacks [19][20][21][14].

claims.believers: Early-2000s forum posts reference the claim that HMB was 'as good as Deca' and a study said to show better results than steroids [20][22]; a 2003 poster described HMB's reputation as a disappointment, comparing it to Deca claims [21].
claims.experts: The ISSN position stand describes benefits as helping reduce muscle damage and promote recovery, not steroid-like effects [1]; a meta-analysis in trained athletes assessed strength and body composition [2].

claims.claim: HMB helps you recover faster and handle more training volume
claims.believers: A T Nation log writer reports that an HMB product helped handle volume and recover between workouts [12].
claims.experts: The ISSN position stand says HMB may help reduce muscle damage and promote recovery [1].

claims.claim: HMB preserves muscle during illness, bed rest or ageing
claims.believers: Some members see HMB as a hedge against muscle loss during hard training or dieting [13][14].
claims.experts: A meta-analysis in older adults and trials of oral nutritional supplements containing HMB in older, malnourished and bed-rested people examined this question [5][6][7][8].

claims.claim: HMB is a safe, low-risk supplement
claims.believers: Users include it routinely among other supplements [14][15].
claims.experts: The ISSN position stand reports chronic use appears safe for up to at least a year and without effects on glucose tolerance [1].
